name: Surrogation
statement: Managers paid on a measure of a strategic goal come to treat the measure as the goal, and pick options that raise it at the goal's expense.
meaning: Surrogation is a claim about belief, not about effort or honesty. A strategic performance measurement system turns a goal such as social ability, or customer satisfaction, into countable measures. Choi, Hecht and Tayler define surrogation as managers losing sight of the construct those measures represent, and acting as though the measures are the construct of interest. They took the label from Yuji Ijiri's 1967 and 1975 books on accounting measurement, which they cite as the source of the idea that a proxy can displace the thing it proxies; those books were not opened for this entry. Their theory borrows Kahneman and Frederick's attribute substitution. A complex target attribute is hard to reach, an easy measure is close to hand, and the easy one gets used. Their footnote 4 keeps the separate label on purpose, to mark the case where a measure built to represent a construct ends up perceived as the construct. The testable part is narrow. Pay a manager on one measure of a goal during one task, then ask for choices in a second task where no money rides on the answer, and the paid measure should still steer the choices.

origin.who: Jongwoon (Willie) Choi, Gary Hecht and William B. Tayler
origin.note: "Lost in Translation: The Effects of Incentive Compensation on Strategy Surrogation" runs to pages 1135 to 1163 of volume 87, issue 4. It names the phenomenon and reports the first two experiments on it. What is read here is the authors' accepted manuscript, dated 24 May 2011 and deposited at BYU ScholarsArchive, where all three authors are at Emory University. The published article itself was not opened.

evidence: Both original experiments ran in the creature-design module of the computer game Spore. Participants built a creature under a stated strategy of maximising its social ability, which four equally weighted measures captured: sing, dance, charm and pose. A quiz forced everyone to state that all four abilities mattered equally before they could continue. Pay for the design task was a flat $10, or $2 for each level of sing alone, or $2 for each level of sing, dance and charm together. Participants then viewed 18 pairs of modification packages for other creatures and chose one from each pair. No money rode on those choices. The surrogation score is the share of choices favouring the previously paid measures over the creature's overall social ability. The main experiment had 79 students from graduate business courses at a highly ranked United States business school, average age 29 and 61% male, split 27 flat wage, 26 single measure and 26 multiple measure. Mean comprehensive surrogation score was 0.59 under single-measure pay against 0.39 under a flat wage, a difference of 0.20, t = 4.56, p < 0.01. Multiple-measure pay gave 0.46 against the single measure's 0.59, a difference of 0.13, t = 2.15, p = 0.02, but on the subset of choices that cost overall social ability the gap was 0.34 against 0.29, t = 0.58, not significant. Multiple-measure pay did not separate from a flat wage, 0.46 against 0.40, t = 1.16, not significant. A follow-up experiment paid participants for the package choices as well, and 24 single-measure participants still scored 0.61 against 26 multiple-measure participants at 0.46, t = 2.31, p = 0.01. The authors report one-sided p-values for their directional predictions and two-sided p-values otherwise.

replication.headline: The core effect has come back three more times on the same task, most strongly in a study of 144 undergraduates, but every one of those studies shares an author with the original.
replication.detail: Choi, Hecht and Tayler adapted their own instrument for three further experiments, reported in the Journal of Accounting Research. They recruited 157, 78 and 92 undergraduates at a BusinessWeek top five business school, average ages 20, 20 and 19, and dropped anyone who had played Spore before, leaving 144, 70 and 83 in the analyses. Experiment 1 put mean comprehensive surrogation at 0.36 under a flat wage and 0.53 under measure-based pay, a difference of 0.17, t = 3.73, p < 0.001. Experiment 3 repeated those two conditions and found 0.36 against 0.46, a difference of 0.10, t = 2.30, p = 0.012. The same paper reports that letting people choose the strategy cut surrogation from 0.53 to 0.48, t = -1.49, p = 0.069, while deliberating over a strategy without choosing it did not, and the authors call that last result surprising. Black, Meservy, Tayler and Williams then removed the pay. In their second experiment, 74 undergraduates who were told only that one skill would be measured scored 0.48 against a control group's 0.36, t = 2.70, p = 0.005, so awareness of measurement was enough on its own. Their first experiment, on 170 Mechanical Turk workers of average age 36, raised cognitive load and raised surrogation-consistent answers with it, t = 2.23, p = 0.014, which they read as evidence that the substitution is nonconscious. Two teams with no overlap with the original authors report surrogation in other tasks. Bentley had experienced chess players bet on games in progress, and Wang, Cheng and Chang ran a 2 x 2 on performance measurement system flexibility. Only the Crossref abstracts of those two papers were read here, so no figure from either appears on this page.

study.cite: Choi, J., Hecht, G., & Tayler, W. B. (2013). Strategy selection, surrogation, and strategic performance measurement systems. Journal of Accounting Research, 51(1), 105-133.

limits: Nobody in any of these experiments was a manager. The samples are graduate business students of average age 29, undergraduates of average ages 20, 19 and 22, and paid workers on Mechanical Turk. Cell sizes in the original run to 24, 26 and 27. All four experimental papers share at least one author with the paper that named the effect, and all of them use variants of one Spore task, so the repeat findings test the theory against the same instrument. No preregistered, multi-site or adversarial replication was located: the search covered Crossref for every work whose title carries the word surrogation, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar records for papers citing the 2012 article, and web search for a direct replication. The dependent variable is a count of choices rather than a reading of belief. Black and colleagues call their own version an admittedly noisy proxy and label the responses surrogation-consistent rather than surrogation. Bentley's chess experiment and Wang, Cheng and Chang's flexibility experiment sit behind the American Accounting Association paywall, which refused automated requests during this check, so their participant counts and results are not stated here. The one field study located is interviews rather than a test: Reinking, Arnold and Sutton spoke to 27 executive to mid-level managers about digital dashboards, and its abstract was read at RePEc rather than in the article. Goodhart's law is the comparison readers ask for, and no primary text of it was read during this check, so the page does not make that comparison.
misreadings: The first error is reading surrogation as gaming. Gaming means hitting the number you are paid for, and the choices that produce the surrogation score carry no payment at all in the main experiment. That design is what separates a changed belief about the objective from a rational response to a contract. The second is treating it as Campbell's law with a new name. Campbell's formulation, that the more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making the more it will distort the process it monitors, appeared in a 1976 Dartmouth occasional paper, reprinted in 2011 and usually cited from its 1979 printing in Evaluation and Program Planning. Campbell introduced his own evidence for it in the same paragraph as "predominantly anecdotal". Surrogation is the narrower claim, and it has experiments. The third is assuming surrogation is always an accident. Reinking, Arnold and Sutton report from interviews that executives design dashboards to produce it deliberately, and argue it can help at operational levels. The fourth is quoting the effect as managers abandoning strategy. Under single-measure pay 0.59 of choices went the surrogating way against 0.39 under a flat wage, so most of the shift sits in choices where surrogating cost nothing.
